lead.t: | Arterial blood gas (ABG) | Is there hypoxaemia or hypercapnia indicating respiratory failure? | PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg in chronic bronchitis suggests advanced disease; normal ABG in mild acute bronchitis. |

b: Measures pH, PaCO2, PaO2 and bicarbonate.
Respiratory acidosis: low pH due to elevated PaCO2.
Chronic respiratory acidosis may show raised bicarbonate due to renal compensation.
Use ABG when there is severe respiratory distress, suspected hypercapnia, unexplained hypoxaemia, shock or need for ventilatory support.

qs.q: A 6-month-old infant with bronchiolitis is tachypneic, wheezing, and using accessory muscles. Arterial blood gas reveals pH 7.31, PaCO2 58 mmHg, and HCO3 24 mEq/L. Which pathophysiological mechanism explains this acid-base disturbance?
o: Excessive lactic acid production from peripheral skeletal muscle fatigue
Renal tubular bicarbonate wasting secondary to systemic viral toxicity
Alveolar hypoventilation due to small airway mucus plugging and trapping
Increased fixed acid load from severe dehydration and tissue hypoxia
Gastrointestinal loss of base equivalents through concurrent diarrhea
qs.e: Inflammation and mucus plugging in bronchiolitis cause air trapping and hypoventilation, leading to carbon dioxide retention and respiratory acidosis.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Paediatrics Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 32-year-old man with advanced HIV infection and a CD4 count of 80 cells/uL develops a subacute fever, dry cough, and progressive hypoxia. Arterial blood gas shows an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. Which diagnostic finding is most consistent with the expected pulmonary pathogen?
o: Acid-fast bacilli detected in bronchoalveolar lavage
Silver-staining cysts identified in induced sputum
Caseating granulomas observed on transbronchial biopsy
Budding yeasts with thick capsules on mucicarmine
Branching hyphae showing acute-angle dichotomous branching
qs.e: Pneumocystis jirovecii presents with hypoxia and elevated A-a gradient, diagnosed via visualization of cysts using methenamine silver.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 45-year-old man undergoes urgent laparotomy for a bleeding duodenal ulcer and receives 12 units of packed red blood cells over three hours. Arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.21, ionized calcium of 0.82 mmol/L, and core body temperature is 34.8 degrees Celsius. Which mechanism primarily links these findings to the administered blood products?
o: Heparin preservation triggering endogenous systemic fibrinolysis cascades
Citrate anticoagulant chelation of plasma ionized divalent calcium ions
Rapid potassium ion leakage from stored cellular erythrocyte membranes
Cold storage physical properties lowering core patient thermal baselines
Acidic supernatant accumulation shifting systemic acid-base equilibrium
qs.e: Citrate in stored blood binds free calcium, directly causing hypocalcaemia during massive transfusion episodes.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: General Surgery Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A trauma patient receives massive transfusion protocol activation following a severe crush injury. Arterial blood gas monitoring reveals a base excess of -8.5 mmol/L and a lactate level of 5.2 mmol/L. Which pathophysiological state is primarily indicated by these metabolic laboratory values?
o: Hepatic dysfunction limiting clearance of circulating lactate.
Renal tubular failure causing impaired hydrogen-ion excretion.
Excessive loss of bicarbonate due to aggressive diuretic use.
Insufficient tissue oxygen delivery compared with metabolic demand.
Failure of respiratory compensation resulting in CO₂ retention.
qs.e: Elevated lactate and negative base excess reflect tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic cellular metabolism.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: General Surgery Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 40-year-old man with poorly controlled Type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with rapid breathing, confusion, and fruity breath odor. Arterial blood gas shows severe metabolic acidosis. Which compensatory mechanism is primarily responsible for restoring his pH?
o: Renal reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in tubules.
Hepatic conversion of excess ketoacids into urea.
Kussmaul breathing driving off carbon dioxide via lungs.
Intracellular buffering via rapid potassium shifts.
Enhanced secretion of titratable acids in nephrons.
qs.e: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis involves hyperventilation to reduce arterial PCO2.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 7-year-old child with severe persistent asthma presents with acute respiratory distress, intercostal retractions, and silent chest on auscultation. Arterial blood gas reveals a rising PCO2. What does this specific finding signify regarding the child's respiratory status?
o: Impending respiratory failure and severe alveolar hypoventilation
Rapidly improving ventilation and effective gas exchange
Adequate metabolic compensation for chronic hypoxia
Paradoxical resolution of bronchospasm in large airways
Normal physiological response to acute beta-agonist use
qs.e: A normal or rising PCO2 in severe asthma indicates fatigued respiratory muscles and impending respiratory failure.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Paediatrics Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: In a study of acid-base balance, a patient's arterial blood gas shows metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. Which underlying condition is the most likely cause?
o: Ingestion of exogenous methanol.
Severe lactic acid accumulation.
Uncontrolled diabetic ketoacidosis.
Proximal renal tubular acidosis.
Advanced chronic renal failure.
qs.e: Renal tubular acidosis causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis due to impaired bicarbonate reabsorption or hydrogen ion excretion.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 48-year-old man in the intensive care unit with severe urosepsis develops sudden hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Arterial blood gas shows a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 120 mmHg, and chest radiography demonstrates bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism causing widespread micro-atelectasis in this patient?
o: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
Loss of surfactant surface‑tension stability
Reduced intrapulmonary arteriolar shunting
Increased alveolar wall compliance
qs.e: In acute respiratory distress syndrome, surfactant dysfunction and loss lead to elevated surface tension and widespread alveolar instability with micro-atelectasis. Hypoxic vasoconstriction and altered compliance are secondary functional consequences rather than the primary cause of alveolar collapse.
qs.s: Introduction to Pulmonary Pathology and Atelectasis: MCQs

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: ABG is the bedside snapshot of oxygenation, ventilation and acid–base status. Interpreting it guides diagnosis, urgency and treatment in common East African illnesses such as pneumonia, TB, malaria and sepsis.

sections.p: An arterial blood gas measures PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH, bicarbonate and calculated values such as base excess. It is obtained from a radial or femoral artery puncture and analysed immediately.

t.b: Is oxygen saturation adequate? SpO₂ < 90% suggests hypoxaemia
Does PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg? Indicates respiratory failure
Is lactate > 2 mmol/L? Suggests shock or severe sepsis

sections.p: Severity is graded by PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH and lactate. In chronic lung disease, PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg with PaO₂ < 60 mmHg signals advanced failure.
b: Acute respiratory failure: PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals the top causes of abnormal ABG are infections (pneumonia, TB, malaria), cardiac failure, sepsis, and drug toxicity.
Patients may be tachypnoeic, cyanotic, confused or hypotensive. Physical signs include wheeze, crackles, JVD or peripheral oedema depending on the underlying disease.
ABG is the cornerstone; adjuncts include chest X‑ray, full blood count, CRP, cultures, HIV test and, where available, ultrasound or ECG.
b: ECG – right heart strain or arrhythmia

t.b: Does PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg? Indicates respiratory failure
Is there consolidation or effusion? Supports pneumonia or TB diagnosis
Positive Gram stain? Guides antibiotic choice
Positive? Increases risk of TB, sepsis and drug interactions

sections.p: Severe acidosis (pH < 7.25), hypercapnia with hypoxaemia, or rising lactate signals impending organ failure and requires urgent intervention.
Treat the underlying cause, correct ventilation and oxygenation, and monitor ABG trends. Supportive care includes fluids, antibiotics and, if available, mechanical ventilation.
b: Monitor ABG every 4–6 hours until stable

sections.p: Repeat ABG after 4–6 hours of treatment to assess response. Prevent complications by early recognition of sepsis, vaccination against pneumococcus and influenza, and malaria prophylaxis.
b: Educate patients on early signs of pneumonia

sections.p: ABG findings can mimic metabolic acidosis from renal failure or diabetic ketoacidosis, and respiratory alkalosis from anxiety or fever.
b: Sepsis – lactic acidosis with normal PaCO₂

sections.p: Pulse oximetry may be falsely normal in severe anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning. ABG may be normal in early COPD exacerbation.
b: Early COPD – ABG normal until hypercapnia develops

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoxaemia (PaO₂ < 50 mmHg), hypercapnia with PaO₂ < 60 mmHg, pH < 7.25, lactate > 4 mmol/L, hypotension < 90/60 mmHg

faq.q: What does a PaCO₂ of 50 mmHg mean?
faq.a: It indicates hypoventilation; look for respiratory failure or COPD exacerbation.

faq.q: Why is a normal ABG reassuring in mild bronchitis?
faq.a: Mild bronchitis usually does not alter ventilation or oxygenation, so ABG remains normal.

faq.q: Can malaria cause an abnormal ABG?
faq.a: Yes, severe malaria can cause metabolic acidosis and hypoxaemia due to anaemia and shock.

exam: A 30‑year‑old man with cough and fever has PaO₂ 55 mmHg and PaCO₂ 48 mmHg. What is the next step? — Give oxygen and start empiric antibiotics for pneumonia; repeat ABG in 4–6 h.
In a patient with sepsis and lactate 3.5 mmol/L, ABG shows pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 65 mmHg. What does this indicate? — Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure; consider mechanical ventilation.
A child with malaria has ABG pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 35 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance? — Metabolic acidosis due to lactic acid build‑up.
Why is pulse oximetry unreliable in severe anaemia? — It measures oxygen saturation of haemoglobin, not the amount of oxygen carried; SpO₂ may appear normal while PaO₂ is low.
When should you avoid aminoglycosides in a patient with abnormal ABG? — If the patient has renal impairment or is on nephrotoxic drugs, as they can worsen acidosis and cause ototoxicity.
In a patient with COPD exacerbation, ABG shows PaCO₂ 55 mmHg and PaO₂ 70 mmHg. What is the likely cause of the low PaO₂? — Hypoventilation leading to CO₂ retention and hypoxaemia.
